root.meaning: a stay, a place to stay, dwelling, inn
root.note: The accusative of mansio, from the verb manēre, ‘to stay, to remain’.

history: A maison was first a place where you stopped. Latin mansio, from manere, ‘to stay’, meant a stay, a place to stay, even an inn. French is unusual here: the TLFi says that mansio means ‘house’ only in Gallo-Romance and in the dialects of the north. Elsewhere, the popular Latin word casa, first ‘hut’, then ‘house’, replaced the classical domus, and Spanish, Italian and Portuguese still say casa. French did not lose casa completely: it hides in chez, as in chez moi, ‘at my place’. Maison itself is attested from the end of the 10th century. The same root gave manoir, ‘manor house’, and French later borrowed mansion straight from Latin.
historyEinfach: Maison comes from the Latin word mansio. It meant ‘a place where you stay’. The verb was manere, ‘to stay’. Other languages took another Latin word, casa: Spanish and Italian say casa for ‘house’. French has this word too, but it is hidden in chez: chez moi means ‘at my home’.

elsewhere.text: Spanish, Italian and Portuguese chose the other Latin word, casa. It is not related to maison, but French has it too, in chez.
